newsitem.title: UK: New UK Conservative leader offers fresh start.
newsitem.headline: New UK Conservative leader offers fresh start.

text.p: William Hague became the youngest leader of Britain's Conservative party in over 200 years on Thursday and promised to put it back on the road to power after Labour's May 1 landslide election victory.
Former Welsh Secretary Hague, 36, won a final ballot for the leadership and promised "nothing short of a revolution" in a party now in opposition after 18 years in government.

"We've had a great setback but let's have no more recriminations. Let's look forward, not back. Let's pick ourselves up, dust ourselves down and return to the future," Hague told members of parliament in his acceptance speech.

Pledging "no grudges" against those who fought against him in a bruising battle for the leadership, he added: "We all start from a clean slate. It is my responsibility to lead this party and it is also my responsibility to heal this party."
His victory was hailed by his two predecessors, former prime ministers John Major and Margaret Thatcher.

Major told MPs and other senior figures at the party's central London headquarters: "What you have done this afternoon is pass the leadership of the Conservative party to the most outstanding political talent in our country today."
Thatcher, who endorsed Hague on the eve of Thursday's final leadership ballot against former chancellor of the exchequer Kenneth Clarke, said: "It's been a good day."
But the new leader was immediately dealt a blow when Clarke rejected an offer of a senior job in Hague's "shadow cabinet".

Clarke said he wanted a break from the political front line after 26 years. "I propose to take an active part in politics from the back benches of the Conservative party, giving my unstinting and loyal support to William Hague," he said.
Clarke's refusal to serve immediately opened up questions about Hague's ability to end the divisions in his party which dogged Major's last days.
Clarke fought a bitter rearguard action from the cabinet to prevent Major bowing to right-wing pressure and ruling out entry into a European single currency.

Hague, who was originally thought to be neither pro- nor anti-Europe, finally came off the fence last week and ruled out entry into a single currency, infuriating pro-Europeans who accused him of doing whatever necessary to win.
Clarke had been the clear-cut leader in two consultative ballots of rank and file party members.

But only the 164 Conservative MPs left after Labour's victory were entitled to vote. Hague won Thursday's vote -- the third and final ballot -- by 92 votes to 70. One MP abstained and another spoilt his ballot paper.

Hague, who first hit the spotlight in 1977 when, as a 16-year-old schoolboy, he brought the Conservative conference to its feet with a rousing speech, promised to change party rules and put himself to a ballot of members later in the year.

"The days of disunity, of factions, of wings, of groups within groups, parties within parties must now come to an end. Our supporters in the country are sick and tired of the Conservatives behaving like a school debating society."
He added that he would not be worried about "putting noses out of joint" if people stepped out of line.
Labour, which hinted before Thursday's ballot it was talking to disaffected pro-Europeans in the Conservative party, was delighted by the result.

Margaret Beckett, Labour's Trade and Industry Secretary, said: "The Tory (Conservative) party has shown that it is more split today than ever before...There are two Tory parties and Mr Hague doesn't know which one he's in."
Minority Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown, also saying he would be happy to welcome anyone who wanted to defect, said the Conservatives had voted for "internal strife".
"This leadership contest has exposed how deep the divisions in the Conservative Party now run," Ashdown said.
